body.en: The EST II Mathematics subject test is a rigorous examination for students in international and American-diploma programmes who wish to demonstrate advanced mathematical competency for university admissions. It covers algebra, geometry, trigonometry, and data analysis at a depth beyond the core EST I test.

label.en: ● Deep Conceptual Intuition — Test format & strategy

body.en: Proportional Invariance, Linear Structure & Quantitative Modeling: Across Egyptian Scholastic Test (EST II — Math Level 1), multi-step problems reduce to identifying invariant quantities—constant rates of change \(m = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\), conservation of total work/mass, or linear system rank conditions. A two-variable linear system \(a_1 x + b_1 y = c_1\), \(a_2 x + b_2 y = c_2\) has a unique intersection if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \ne \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\), no solution (parallel lines) if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \ne \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\), and infinitely many solutions if all three ratios coincide.

body.en: EST II Math is taken as a standalone subject test on the EST II examination day. It contains both multiple-choice and short constructed-response questions. The content aligns closely with pre-calculus and advanced secondary mathematics.

label.en: ⏱ EST II Math Level 1 Pacing & Calculator Strategy

body.en:
• Pacing Baseline: 50 questions in 60 minutes = 72 seconds per question. There is zero negative marking — never leave any question blank.
  • Three-Pass Execution: Pass 1 (Qs 1–25, ~20 min): bank routine algebra, basic trigonometry, and straight arithmetic. Pass 2 (Qs 26–45, ~25 min): solve conic equations, solid geometry, and multi-step probability. Pass 3 (Qs 46–50 & review, ~15 min): tackle non-routine proofs, vectors, and ensure all grid-in/bubble items are complete.
  • Calculator Mastery: An approved scientific or graphing calculator is permitted throughout. Use it to verify complex number computations, evaluate trigonometric functions in proper degree/radian modes, and solve quadratic systems.

label.en: ▲ The 4 Core Commandments for Scoring 750+ on EST II Math

body.en:
• 1. Never Leave Unanswered Items: With no penalty for incorrect answers, eliminate obvious extremes and make an educated guess whenever stumped.
  • 2. Verify Calculator Angle Mode: Trig questions in EST II frequently switch between radian measure (e.g., \(5\pi/6\)) and degree measure (e.g., \(150°\)). Confirm angle mode before performing numerical evaluations.
  • 3. Conic Identification by Inspection: Check the coefficients of \(x^2\) and \(y^2\): equal signs and equal coefficients indicate a circle; equal signs but different coefficients indicate an ellipse; opposite signs indicate a hyperbola.
  • 4. Memorize 3D Solid & Circle Relations: Sphere volume \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\) and surface area \(4\pi r^2\); cone volume \(\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\); inscribed circle angle \(=\frac{1}{2}\text{central}\); cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles sum to \(180°\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Test format & strategy)

body.en:
Why Successive Multipliers & Harmonic Average Speed Work: If a quantity \(Q_0\) undergoes a percentage change \(p\%\) followed by \(q\%\), the compound multiplier is the product of individual scale factors:

\[ Q_{\text{final}} = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{100}\right) = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p + q}{100} + \frac{pq}{10000}\right) \]

Notice the cross term \(\dfrac{pq}{10000}\): an increase of \(p\%\) followed by a decrease of \(p\%\) yields \(Q_0\bigl(1 - (p/100)^2\bigr) < Q_0\). Similarly, traveling equal distance \(d\) at speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) takes total time \(T = \frac{d}{v_1} + \frac{d}{v_2}\), so average speed is the harmonic mean \(v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

label.en: Worked Example A — Test format & strategy (Medium Application)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): In the diagram below, lines AB and CD are parallel. Line EF is a transversal intersecting AB at G and CD at H. If the measure of angle AGH is \( (2x + 10)^{\circ} \) and the measure of angle GHD is \( (3x - 5)^{\circ} \), find the value of x.

Step-by-Step Solution: Since lines AB and CD are parallel and EF is a transversal, angle AGH and angle GHD are consecutive interior angles. Consecutive interior angles are supplementary, meaning their measures add up to \( 180^{\circ} \). Therefore, we can set up the equation: \( (2x + 10)^{\circ} + (3x - 5)^{\circ} = 180^{\circ} \) Combine like terms: \( 5x + 5 = 180 \) Subtract 5 from both sides: \( 5x = 175 \) Divide by 5: \( x = \frac{175}{5} \) \( x = 35 \) Let's check the angles: Angle AGH = \( 2(35) + 10 = 70 + 10 = 80^{\circ} \) Angle GHD = \( 3(35) - 5 = 105 - 5 = 100^{\circ} \) \( 80^{\circ} + 100^{\circ} = 180^{\circ} \), which confirms our value of x. Common algebraic trap: Students might incorrectly assume the angles are equal (alternate interior or corresponding angles) or misapply the supplementary property. For example, setting \( 2x + 10 = 180 \) or \( 3x - 5 = 180 \). Final Answer: 25.

label.en: Worked Example \(B\) — Test format & strategy (Medium Application)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): The first term of a geometric sequence is \(a\). The common ratio is \(r\). The sum of the first 3 terms is 21, and the sum of the first 6 terms is 189. If \(r > 0\), find the value of \(a\) and \(r\).

Step-by-Step Solution: Let the geometric sequence be denoted by \(a_n\), where \(a_1 = a\) and the common ratio is \(r\). The sum of the first \(n\) terms of a geometric sequence is given by \(S_n = \frac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}\) (for \(r \neq 1\)). We are given that \(S_3 = 21\) and \(S_6 = 189\). So, we have the equations: 1) \(\frac{a(r^3 - 1)}{r - 1} = 21\) 2) \(\frac{a(r^6 - 1)}{r - 1} = 189\) We can rewrite \(r^6 - 1\) using the difference of squares factorization: \(r^6 - 1 = (r^3)^2 - 1^2 = (r^3 - 1)(r^3 + 1)\). Substitute this into the second equation: \(\frac{a(r^3 - 1)(r^3 + 1)}{r - 1} = 189\) Now, we can see that \(\frac{a(r^3 - 1)}{r - 1}\) is part of this expression, which is equal to 21 from equation (1). So, we can substitute 21 into the modified second equation: \(21(r^3 + 1) = 189\) Divide both sides by 21: \(r^3 + 1 = \frac{189}{21}\) \(r^3 + 1 = 9\) Subtract 1 from both sides: \(r^3 = 8\) Since \(r > 0\), we take the real cube root: \(r = \sqrt[3]{8}\) \(r = 2\) Now, substitute \(r=2\) back into the first equation to find \(a\): \(\frac{a(2^3 - 1)}{2 - 1} = 21\) \(\frac{a(8 - 1)}{1} = 21\) \(a(7) = 21\) Divide by 7: \(a = \frac{21}{7}\) \(a = 3\) Thus, the value of \(a\) is 3 and the value of \(r\) is 2. Let's check the common misconceptions: - If \(r=1\), then \(S_n = na\). \(S_3 = 3a = 21 \implies a=7\). \(S_6 = 6a = 6(7) = 42 \neq 189\). So \(r \neq 1\). - Common algebraic errors might involve incorrect factorization of \(r^6-1\) or misinterpreting the sums. Final Answer: \(a=3, r=2\).

label.en: Worked Example \(C\) — Test format & strategy (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): A right circular cone has a height of \( 12 \) cm. A smaller cone is formed by slicing the top of the larger cone with a plane parallel to the base. The smaller cone is similar to the larger cone, and its height is \( 6 \) cm. If the radius of the base of the larger cone is \( 9 \) cm, what is the radius of the base of the smaller cone?

Step-by-Step Solution: Let the larger cone be denoted by \( C_1 \) and the smaller cone by \( C_2 \). The height of \( C_1 \) is \( H_1 = 12 \) cm and its radius is \( R_1 = 9 \) cm. The height of \( C_2 \) is \( H_2 = 6 \) cm. Since the smaller cone is similar to the larger cone, the ratio of their corresponding linear dimensions is constant. Therefore, the ratio of their heights is equal to the ratio of their radii. \[ \frac{R_2}{R_1} = \frac{H_2}{H_1} \] Substitute the given values: \[ \frac{R_2}{9 \text{ cm}} = \frac{6 \text{ cm}}{12 \text{ cm}} \] \[ \frac{R_2}{9} = \frac{1}{2} \] To find \( R_2 \), multiply both sides by 9: \[ R_2 = 9 \times \frac{1}{2} \] \[ R_2 = 4.5 \text{ cm} \] The radius of the base of the smaller cone is \( 4.5 \) cm.

label.en: Worked Example \(D\) — Test format & strategy (Hard Application)

body.en:
Problem (Hard): \( P(A) = 0.4 \) and \( P(B|A) = 0.5 \). Find \( P(A \cap B) \).

Step-by-Step Solution: \( P(A\cap B) = P(B|A)\cdot P(A) = 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.2 \). Final Answer: \( 0.2 \).

question.en: An EST II Mathematics examination consists of 50 questions with an allocated testing time of 60 minutes. If a student completes the first 30 questions in 33 minutes, what is the maximum average time, in seconds, the student can spend on each of the remaining 20 questions?

solution.en:
Step 1: Compute total available time in seconds: \[ 60\text{ min} \times 60\text{ s/min} = 3600\text{ seconds}. \]

Step 2: Compute time spent on first 30 questions: \[ 33\text{ min} \times 60\text{ s/min} = 1980\text{ seconds}. \]

Step 3: Calculate remaining time: \[ 3600 - 1980 = 1620\text{ seconds}. \]

Step 4: Determine average time per remaining question: \[ \frac{1620\text{ seconds}}{20\text{ questions}} = 81\text{ seconds per question}. \]

question.en: On the EST II Math exam, Advanced Algebra and Functions together account for 40% of the questions. In a 50-question test, if a student targets an accuracy rate of 90% in these two high-yield domains, how many questions from these domains can the student afford to miss at most?

solution.en:
Step 1: Find total questions from Advanced Algebra and Functions: \[ 50 \times 0.40 = 20\text{ questions}. \]

Step 2: Calculate 90% accuracy target: \[ 20 \times 0.90 = 18\text{ questions correct}. \]

Step 3: Find maximum allowed missed questions: \[ 20 - 18 = 2\text{ questions}. \]

question.en: [Practice 3 · Hard] In the diagram, \( \triangle ABC \) is a right-angled triangle with the right angle at \( C \). The length of the hypotenuse \( AB \) is \( 26 \) units. Point \( D \) lies on \( AB \) such that \( CD \) is the altitude to the hypotenuse. If \( AD = 4 \) units and \( BD = x \) units, find the value of \( x \).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Test format & strategy and start from \( \triangle ABC \).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( \triangle ADC \sim \triangle CDB \sim \triangle ACB \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

solution.en: In a right-angled triangle, the altitude to the hypotenuse creates similar triangles. Specifically, \( riangle ADC \sim riangle CDB \sim riangle ACB \). Using the property that the square of the altitude is equal to the product of the segments of the hypotenuse (geometric mean theorem), we have \( CD^2 = AD imes BD \). Alternatively, we can use the similarity between \( riangle ADC \) and \( riangle CDB \): \( rac{AD}{CD} = rac{CD}{BD} \) which leads to \( CD^2 = AD imes BD \). We also know that in a right-angled triangle, the square of one leg is equal to the product of the hypotenuse and the projection of that leg onto the hypotenuse. For leg \( AC \): \( AC^2 = AD imes AB \). For leg \( BC \): \( BC^2 = BD imes AB \). We are given \( AB = 26 \) and \( AD = 4 \). The length of the hypotenuse \( AB = AD + BD \). So, \( 26 = 4 + x \), which means \( x = 22 \). Alternatively, using the property \( BC^2 = BD imes AB \): We can first find \( AC^2 = AD imes AB = 4 imes 26 = 104 \). Then \( BC^2 = AB^2 - AC^2 = 26^2 - 104 = 676 - 104 = 572 \). Now, \( BC^2 = BD imes AB \) gives \( 572 = x imes 26 \). \( x = rac{572}{26} = 22 \). A common algebraic trap is to incorrectly apply the geometric mean theorem for the legs. For instance, some might assume \( AC = AD \) or \( BC = BD \), or try to relate \( AD \) and \( BD \) directly using the lengths of the legs without considering the hypotenuse. The value of \( x = BD = 22 \). Answer: \( 22 \).
